article.overview: An ultraviolet spectrometer measures how strongly a target emits, reflects or absorbs light at each wavelength in the ultraviolet band, which is shorter than visible light. Ultraviolet signatures help scientists identify gases, surface frosts and other materials, and they are especially useful at wavelengths that Earth's atmosphere strongly absorbs. Two lunar-related examples are documented here: the Apollo 16 far-ultraviolet camera/spectrograph, which was set up on the lunar surface in April 1972 [4][6], and the Lyman Alpha Mapping Project (LAMP) on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, which maps the Moon from orbit [1]. The catalogue assigns this payload to 'Mineralogical and chemical analysis'. That assignment is retained unchanged, although ultraviolet spectrometers are mainly remote-sensing instruments.
article.description: An ultraviolet spectrometer is an optical instrument that separates ultraviolet light into its component wavelengths and records how bright each wavelength is. Most instruments in this class collect light from a target through a telescope or slit, disperse it with a grating or equivalent optical element, and record the spectrum with a detector. Some ultraviolet instruments also record images, so each point in an image carries spectral information. LAMP is described as an imaging ultraviolet spectrometer [1]. The Apollo 16 instrument, whose title combines 'camera' and 'spectrograph', recorded far-ultraviolet images on photographic film using an electronographic technique [4].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The stated purpose of LAMP is to map the Moon's surface in far-ultraviolet light, to look for surface ice and frost near the poles, and to image permanently shadowed regions, which receive little or no direct sunlight [1]. Building up data over the mission is described as allowing surface resolutions of a few kilometres [1]. The Apollo 16 instrument was used for far-ultraviolet observations of Earth from the lunar surface, and its Earth-observation results were reported by Carruthers and Page in 1972 [5]. Published results included the first far-ultraviolet image of Earth taken from a distance, polar auroras and the tropical airglow belt [6]. Lunar-atmosphere and observatory-site goals appear in secondary sources but are not verified here and are not claimed.
article.operating_principle: In general terms, an ultraviolet spectrometer gathers light from a target through an aperture or slit, separates the wavelengths with a diffraction grating or equivalent element, and records the intensity at each wavelength. An imaging spectrometer records this spectral information for each position in a scene, so that the composition of different surface areas can be compared. The Apollo 16 instrument instead used an electronographic technique to record ultraviolet images on photographic film, and the film was brought back to Earth [4][6]. The specific optical design of each instrument is not verified in the sources accessible to this article. Because the Moon has only a negligible atmosphere, an instrument on the surface or in lunar orbit is not subject to the atmospheric absorption that limits ultraviolet observations from Earth.
article.scientific_importance: LAMP was designed to search for surface ice and frost near the poles and to image permanently shadowed regions [1]. Mapping where such volatile materials occur helps scientists evaluate the lunar surface, but the scientific yield of LAMP's published mission results is outside the verified scope of this article. The Apollo 16 instrument showed that a hand-deployed telescope on the lunar surface could record far-ultraviolet images of Earth, polar auroras and airglow [6], and APS News describes it as the first telescope set up on another planetary body [6]. Together the two examples illustrate ultraviolet spectroscopy in two configurations: surface observation during a crewed mission, and continuous orbital mapping from a spacecraft.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for an ultraviolet spectrometer. The two examples below are a modern orbital imaging spectrometer (LAMP) and a historical surface-deployed far-ultraviolet camera/spectrograph (Apollo 16). Their mass, power and optics are not directly comparable: one is an orbital instrument carried within a spacecraft power and thermal budget, and the other was a manually aimed, film-recording instrument. Values below are tied to the named instrument and source.

examples.name: Lyman Alpha Mapping Project (LAMP), Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
examples.summary: LAMP is described as an imaging ultraviolet spectrometer that detects ultraviolet light between 1,200 and 1,800 Angstrom, which is 120 to 180 nm [1]. The reported instrument mass is 6.1 kg (13 lb) and the average power is 4.0 W [1]. Search-result summaries of SwRI material, which could not be confirmed against the primary SwRI documents, give a measured mass of 4.4 kg, a maximum power of 3.9 W, minimum requirements of 6.1 kg and 4.5 W, a first-order passband of 57.5 to 196.5 nm, an effective area of 1.3 plus or minus 0.4 square cm at 121.6 nm, a spectral resolution of 0.182 nm, a slit field of view of 0.31 by 6.00 degrees, and heritage from the ALICE instrument on New Horizons [2][3]. These values are reported here as unverified and are not treated as established specifications.
examples.qualification: Mass and power are mission-level figures from a secondary mission page. They should be confirmed against NASA or PDS documentation before use in any formal comparison.

examples.name: Apollo 16 far-ultraviolet camera/spectrograph
examples.mass_as_reported: 'the 50-pound telescope' [6]; 50 lb converted to approximately 22.7 kg for this table
examples.passband_as_reported: Not verified in primary sources; secondary search summaries conflict and are not used
examples.summary: The Apollo 16 far-ultraviolet camera/spectrograph was set up on the lunar surface by John Young in the Descartes Highlands, and Young and Charles Duke pointed it by hand at Earth and space targets [6]. APS News describes it as a 50-pound telescope, which corresponds to about 22.7 kg [6]. The NASA technical record gives operation from 21 to 23 April 1972 [4], after the landing on 20 April 1972 [6]. It used an electronographic technique to record far-ultraviolet images on film [4], and nearly 200 images were brought back to Earth [6]. Its wavelength range, optical parameters (focal ratio, aperture and field of view), dimensions and power are not verified in the primary sources accessible to this article. Secondary sources give conflicting wavelength limits, which are not used here.
examples.qualification: The mass figure is a rounded approximation from a popular-science account. The NASA technical record [4] confirms the author, title, journal and operating dates but does not state the mass.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No verified dimensions are available for either example. The Apollo 16 instrument is described only through its mass [6], and its enclosure size and proportions are not verified here. A new ultraviolet spectrometer's dimensions would be set by its optical path (telescope length, grating and detector geometry), field of view and mounting, and would need to be specified for the instrument concerned.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The reported masses are 6.1 kg for LAMP [1] and about 22.7 kg (50 lb) for the Apollo 16 instrument [6]. The conflicting LAMP values (4.4 kg measured; 6.1 kg minimum requirement) are unverified [2][3]. The two instruments differ in design, era and platform, so their masses should not be compared as like-for-like.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: LAMP's average power is reported as 4.0 W [1]. A maximum of 3.9 W and a minimum requirement of 4.5 W appear only in unverified summaries [2][3]. No verified power value was found for the Apollo 16 instrument in the sources accessed, so its power requirement is reported as not publicly specified here.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: An ultraviolet spectrometer on the Moon must tolerate vacuum, extreme thermal cycling between lunar day and night, radiation and micrometeoroid exposure, and it must keep its optics clean. A surface-based instrument also needs a stable support and a means of pointing. An orbiting instrument must maintain pointing and sensor temperature within its spacecraft's power and thermal budget. Specific LAMP and Apollo 16 environmental tolerances are not verified in this article's sources, so none are stated here.
article.limitations: The ultraviolet spectrometer class covers instruments with different wavelength ranges, optics, mass and operating modes, so no single performance envelope applies. LAMP and the Apollo 16 camera differ in platform, era and recording method. Specifications for both examples are incomplete in the primary sources accessible to this article, and some reported values conflict. The Apollo 16 wavelength range and optical parameters are not verified, and LAMP sensitivity, spectral resolution and field of view are given only as unverified secondary summaries.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: The two examples were delivered by different routes. LAMP was an instrument on an orbiting spacecraft [1], while the Apollo 16 instrument was a surface payload set up by astronauts [6]. The orbital route is the more relevant model for a new ultraviolet spectrometer that would operate from orbit; the surface route applies to a surface-deployed instrument.
transportation_process: Integrate the instrument into a spacecraft on Earth. LAMP was carried on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter [1].
Launch on a launch vehicle. LRO flew on an Atlas V, per the Spaceflight Now mission page [1].
For an orbiter, transfer to the Moon and enter lunar orbit. The LRO trajectory and orbit-insertion details are not verified in this article.
Commission and operate the instrument within the spacecraft's pointing, thermal and data systems. These LAMP interfaces are not verified.
For a surface instrument, carry it on a lunar lander and deploy it. The Apollo 16 instrument was set up by its crew and pointed by hand [6].
Confirm mass, power, thermal, pointing and data interfaces before assigning any new instrument to a specific lander or spacecraft.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The Apollo 16 instrument was deployed by astronauts on the surface, set up in the Descartes Highlands and pointed by hand [6]. LAMP was not deployed on the surface; it operated from lunar orbit as part of LRO [1]. Its deployment details are not verified here.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 16 (April 1972) is the surface example [4][6]. LRO's LAMP is the orbital example [1].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No verified compatibility with any named lander or spacecraft is given. For LAMP, the instrument is documented as flying on LRO [1], but LRO's interface data are not verified in this article. For a new instrument, the mass, power, dimensions, mounting, thermal, pointing and data requirements must be compared with verified spacecraft specifications before compatibility is assessed.

article.historical_significance: The Apollo 16 far-ultraviolet camera/spectrograph was used on the lunar surface in April 1972. Its images included the first far-ultraviolet image of Earth taken from a distance, polar auroras and the tropical airglow belt, and APS News describes it as the first telescope set up on another planetary body [6]. Its results were published by Carruthers in Applied Optics in 1973 [4] and by Carruthers and Page in Science in 1972 [5]. LAMP, flown on LRO, is significant as a lunar ultraviolet mapping instrument, but the published results of that mission lie outside this article's verified scope [1].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The catalogue category 'Mineralogical and chemical analysis' is the catalogue assignment and does not describe ultraviolet spectrometers as a whole, many of which are remote-sensing instruments. Key LAMP values conflict across sources: mass (6.1 kg versus a 4.4 kg measured value) and passband (1,200 to 1,800 Angstrom versus 57.5 to 196.5 nm) [1][2][3]. The Apollo 16 wavelength range is not verified. No direct image asset URL could be verified for either example, so this article contains no images. The primary LAMP instrument paper in Space Science Reviews [7] was identified but could not be accessed; it is the first document to check for verified specifications. No landing-site or lander-compatibility recommendations are made.

LAMP values from search-result summaries only, not verified against primary text: effective area 1.3 plus or minus 0.4 cm2 at 121.6 nm, spectral resolution 0.182 nm, slit field of view 0.31 by 6.00 degrees, detector type, 40 by 40 mm entrance aperture, and ALICE heritage [2][3]. These are not included as verified specifications.

Apollo 16 wavelength range unverified: secondary search summaries conflict (500 to 1600 Angstrom and 'below 1600 Angstrom'). The NASA technical record [4] and APS News [6] do not state a wavelength range. Focal ratio, aperture and field of view are also unverified; a low-reliability mirror giving f/1.0, 75 mm and a 20 degree field was not used.
Apollo 16 dimensions and power are not verified. Mass of about 50 lb (about 22.7 kg) comes from APS News [6] and is a rounded popular-science figure.
The Applied Optics paper [4] and the Science paper [5] were not opened. The NTRS record confirmed title, author, journal and date only.
The primary LAMP instrument paper in Space Science Reviews [7] was identified but not accessed; the DOI link redirected to a login page in the direct fetch attempt.
